price.source: Zomato cost for two (₹, as listed)

ratings.source: Google Maps rating and review count

demand.source: Google Trends, Rajasthan (index within each query set)

findings.headline: of all Google reviews go to the top 10% of cafés.
findings.body: Everyone else shares a thin slice of attention, so each new review counts for more. Asking happy customers for one is the cheapest way up.
findings.limit: It doesn't say the most-reviewed cafés are the best, only that they are found the most.
how: The typical café has 85 Google reviews; 52% have fewer than a hundred.
I sorted the 392 cafés with Google reviews from most reviewed to least and added up the top tenth.
Resampling the cafés 2,000 times puts the share between 60% and 72% (95% interval).
The Gini coefficient, a 0-to-1 measure of how unevenly something is shared, is 0.79. Zero would mean every café had the same number of reviews.

findings.headline: of cafés have 10 or more cafés within a 5-minute walk.
findings.body: Customers here always have a choice next door. Location alone won't set a café apart; what it offers has to.
findings.limit: It doesn't say whether a crowded street helps or hurts a café's trade.
how: For each of the 456 mapped cafés I counted the others within 500 metres, about a five-minute walk. The typical café has 40.
Cafés sit closer together than chance would put them: 33% in C-Scheme, 43% in Malviya Nagar.
To test for clustering I compared the average distance to the nearest café with what the same number of cafés, scattered at random over the same ground, would give (the Clark-Evans test).
C-Scheme: 53 m observed against 79 m at random; Malviya Nagar: 84 m observed against 147 m at random. Gaps this large would arise by chance less than one time in a hundred.

findings.headline: of cafés with under 10 reviews rate 4.8 or more.
findings.body: With 1,000+ reviews, just 6% do. A perfect score on a few reviews is mostly luck: judge any rating, yours or a rival's, by the reviews behind it.
findings.limit: It doesn't say new cafés inflate their scores; a few reviews simply swing more.
how: I grouped the 380 rated cafés by how many reviews they have and took the share rated 4.8 or above in each group.
Ratings also spread less as reviews grow: the typical gap from the group average falls from 0.6 stars to 0.24.

Across all cafés, more reviews go with a lower rating (rank correlation -0.36; a shuffle test puts the chance of this by luck below 0.001). This is regression to the mean, not a sign that popular cafés are worse.

findings.headline: of cafés rate higher on Google than on Zomato.
findings.body: By about 0.4 stars for the very same café. Compare yourself with cafés on the same app, never across apps.
findings.limit: It doesn't say which app is right, only that their scores are not interchangeable.
how: I took the 101 cafés rated on both Google and Zomato dine-in and subtracted one rating from the other, café by café.
Resampling those cafés 4,000 times puts the average gap between 0.27 and 0.47 stars (95% interval), clear of zero.
9% score the same on both; 20% score higher on Zomato.

findings.headline: of cafés on Zomato get more delivery reviews than dine-in reviews.
findings.body: For most cafés, the delivery order shapes the reputation more than the table does. Packaging and delivery time deserve the same care as the room.
findings.limit: It doesn't say delivery earns more than the dining room, only that it is reviewed more.
how: For the 201 cafés listed on Zomato I compared each café's count of delivery reviews with its dine-in reviews. 75% have at least one delivery review.
The share is between 50% and 63% (95% Wilson interval).

findings.headline: of the Wi-Fi review boost disappears when you compare similar cafés.
findings.body: Cafés with Wi-Fi get 2.5× the reviews, mostly because they tend to offer more of everything. Wi-Fi alone won't bring reviews. The one feature that still stands out is kid-friendly.
findings.limit: It doesn't say Wi-Fi is worthless; customers may still choose a café for it.
how: All cafés: the median Google reviews of cafés that list a feature against those that don't, for the 133 cafés on Zomato with a listed price. Cafés with Wi-Fi list 3.7 other features on average, against 2.5 for the rest.

Similar cafés: a regression on the logarithm of reviews that holds area, café type and price level fixed, so each feature is compared against cafés that are otherwise alike. Wi-Fi: +48% (90% interval -17% to +190% from 3,000 resamples).

Kid-friendly: +403% across all cafés, +219% among similar ones; Smoking area: +208% across all cafés, -12% among similar ones; Board games or books: +171% across all cafés, +20% among similar ones; Wi-Fi or work-friendly: +148% across all cafés, +48% among similar ones; Breakfast: +62% across all cafés, +15% among similar ones; Outdoor seating: +40% across all cafés, +14% among similar ones; Home delivery: -12% across all cafés, -15% among similar ones; Vegetarian only: -16% across all cafés, +25% among similar ones.
This is association, not cause: a listing can mark the kind of café that draws reviews without drawing them itself.

findings.headline: of cafés charge ₹500 or less for two.
findings.body: Price has no link to rating: dearer cafés rate no higher, cheaper ones no lower. Price for your customer, not for your score.
findings.limit: It doesn't say price doesn't matter to customers, only that it doesn't predict the rating.
how: Cost for two as listed on Zomato, for 183 cafés. The typical café charges ₹600: ₹700 in C-Scheme and ₹500 in Malviya Nagar.
Price against Google rating, for 132 cafés: rank correlation -0.13, where zero means no link and ±1 a perfect one. A shuffle test finds nothing (chance of a link this size by luck: 0.12).
Price does go with more reviews, weakly; dearer cafés tend to be bigger.

findings.headline: of cafés list 5 or more cuisines.
findings.body: More list fast food (62%) than coffee (49%). A short, focused menu stands out simply by being rare.
findings.limit: It doesn't say a short menu does better, only that it is rarer.
how: The typical menu spans 7 cuisines. The cuisine tags each of 201 cafés lists on Zomato. 'Café' and 'Beverages', which nearly all list, are left out of the chart.

findings.headline: of cafés show up on only one app.
findings.body: Only 40% are on Zomato and 15% on Swiggy. Every app a café is missing from is a crowd that never sees it.
findings.limit: It doesn't count apps outside Google Maps, Zomato, Swiggy and magicpin.
how: 77% on Google Maps; 40% on Zomato; 15% on Swiggy.
Each of the 506 cafés matched across the platform searches I run on every update.
Absent means it did not appear in our searches of that platform, which is how a customer browsing the area would miss it too.

profiles.name: Town Coffee
profiles.tagline: The coffee house Jaipur works from.

story.text: Built for staying: fast Wi-Fi and a room full of laptops made the Malviya Nagar café, near World Trade Park, a go-to for people who work remotely.

source.title: Town Coffee in Jaipur: Perfect Cafe for Digital Nomads

story.text: A menu that goes beyond the cup, with mezze platters, sandwiches and baked pasta alongside coffee and cold drinks: somewhere you can stay for lunch, not just a latte.

source.title: Town Coffee in Jaipur: Perfect Cafe for Digital Nomads

story.text: The format has travelled: Town Coffee now appears in both areas we track, Malviya Nagar and C-Scheme.
